title: Volcanoes: Mountains of Fire
summary: How volcanoes form, why they erupt in different ways, how scientists watch them, and what the old lava fields of western Arabia tell us.
poll: People should never live near a volcano.

versions.title: Mountains of Fire
versions.text:
A volcano is a hole in the ground. Hot rock comes out of it. The rock is so hot it melts. Deep down, it is called magma. When it comes out, it is lava. Lava can glow red. Then it cools. It gets hard.

The top of the Earth is cut in big parts. They are called plates. The plates move a bit each year. Most volcanoes are at the edge of a plate. A few sit on a hot spot. This is a hot place in the midst of a plate.

Some erupt with a big bang. Ash and rock shoot up high. Some are calm. Their lava flows out. It is like a slow red stream.

Scientists watch them. Does the ground shake? Does it swell up? They test the gas, too. Then they warn folks in time.

The west of Saudi Arabia has old lava fields. They are called harrat. The rock there is black. In 1256, lava came near the town of Madinah. But it stopped. It did not get to the town.

versions.title: Mountains of Fire
versions.text:
A volcano is an opening in the ground. Hot rock comes up through it. The rock is so hot that it has melted. Deep under the ground, this rock is called magma. When it comes out at the top, we call it lava. Fresh lava glows red and orange. As it cools, it turns into hard, dark rock.

The outside of the Earth is broken into huge pieces. They are called plates. The plates move very slowly. They move as fast as your nails grow. Most volcanoes form at the edges of plates. A few form in the middle of a plate. They sit on a hot spot. There, extra heat comes up from deep down.

Not all volcanoes erupt in the same way. Some blow up with a loud blast. Ash, gas, and rock shoot high into the sky. Others are calm. Their runny lava pours out. It flows down the hill like a slow, red stream.

Scientists watch volcanoes. They check for small shakes in the ground. They see if the ground swells up. They test the gas that comes out, too. When the signs change, they warn people. Then people can move to a safe place.

In the west of Saudi Arabia, there are wide fields of old lava. They are called harrat. The land has dark rock and small, round hills. In 1256, lava flowed close to the city of Madinah. It stopped. It did not reach the city.

In 2009, thousands of small earthquakes shook Harrat Lunayyir as magma moved underground, so some nearby villages were evacuated for a time. versions.title: Volcanoes: Mountains of Fire
versions.text:
A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust through which extraordinarily hot, molten rock escapes from deep underground. While this molten material remains confined beneath the surface, geologists refer to it as magma. Once it emerges onto the ground, it is classified as lava. Freshly erupted lava is hot enough to glow brilliant red and orange, and as it gradually cools, it solidifies into dark volcanic rock that may dominate the surrounding landscape for thousands of years.

The outer shell of our planet is divided into enormous sections called tectonic plates, which migrate extremely slowly, typically only a few centimeters annually. The majority of volcanoes develop along the boundaries separating these plates. Where two plates diverge, as they do beneath Iceland, magma rises to occupy the widening gap between them. Where one plate descends beneath another, rock deep underground begins to melt, and the less dense magma gradually forces its way toward the surface. A long chain of such volcanoes encircles the Pacific Ocean, a region known as the Ring of Fire. Certain volcanoes, however, originate in the interior of a plate, above a hot spot where unusually intense heat ascends from far inside the Earth. The Hawaiian Islands formed in sequence as the Pacific Plate gradually traveled across one such hot spot.

Volcanoes do not all erupt in identical ways. Some produce explosive eruptions that propel ash, gas, and fragmented rock high into the atmosphere. This typically occurs when the magma is viscous, meaning thick and sticky, because dissolved gas becomes trapped inside it until the accumulated pressure is abruptly released. Other volcanoes behave considerably more calmly. Their thin, fluid lava allows gas to escape relatively easily, so it pours out steadily and travels downhill like a slow, luminous river. A volcano that has been inactive for a long period but could still erupt is described as dormant.

Scientists continuously monitor active and dormant volcanoes using specialized instruments. Seismometers record the minor earthquakes generated as magma migrates underground. Meanwhile, satellites and precise ground sensors detect whether the surface is gradually swelling as magma accumulates below. Researchers also analyze the gases escaping from fissures, since changes in their amount or chemistry can indicate rising magma. When these warning signals change rapidly, authorities can evacuate surrounding communities before an eruption begins.

In western Saudi Arabia, extensive fields of ancient lava known as harrat cover the land with dark, jagged rock and low cone-shaped hills. Geologists connect these fields to the gradual widening of the Red Sea, which is slowly separating Arabia from Africa. In 1256, a volcano southeast of Madinah erupted for several weeks. Its lava advanced toward the city before halting short of it. In 2009, thousands of small earthquakes shook Harrat Lunayyir as magma pushed upward underground, and some nearby villages were temporarily evacuated as a precaution. No eruption followed, but geologists continue to monitor the region closely.

LOW.prompt: Scientists watch volcanoes so they can warn people. Explain two signs scientists look for and why each one matters.
checklist: I named two warning signs from the article.
I explained why each sign helps keep people safe.
I wrote in complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: Scientists watch volcanoes for warning signs to warn people before it is too late. One sign is that the ground can shake with tiny earthquakes as magma moves underground, and this tells scientists an eruption might be coming. Another sign is that the ground can swell up as magma and lava collect below the surface. These signs matter because they help scientists warn people near the tectonic plate boundary in time to move to safety before a volcano can erupt.

questions.stem: Why do some volcanoes erupt with a violent blast?
options: Their thin, runny lava lets gas escape too quickly
They sit far from plate boundaries, above a hot spot
Scientists stopped monitoring them for many years
Thick, sticky magma traps gas until it bursts free
questions.why: The article explains that gas gets trapped in thick, sticky magma until the pressure bursts free.

wrong.A: Runny lava that lets gas escape leads to calm eruptions.
wrong.B: Being above a hot spot does not explain a violent blast.
wrong.C: Monitoring does not cause or stop eruptions.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: "Scientists monitor active volcanoes." What does monitor mean?
options: To repair something that is broken
To watch and check over time
To build something new
To make something stop
questions.why: The paragraph describes scientists recording earthquakes, measuring the ground, and testing gases again and again, which is watching and checking over time.

wrong.D: Scientists cannot stop a volcano from erupting.

questions.stem: What happens where two plates pull apart, as they do in Iceland?
options: Magma rises to fill the gap
One plate slides under the other
A hot spot forms in the middle
The lava turns straight into ash
questions.why: The article says that where two plates pull apart, magma rises to fill the widening gap.

wrong.B: Sliding under happens where plates push together, not where they pull apart.
wrong.C: Hot spots are in the middle of a plate, not at its edges.
wrong.D: The article does not say lava turns into ash there.

questions.stem: Why do scientists most likely keep watching the harrat today?
options: Lava is flowing into Madinah right now
They want to collect the black rock to sell
The area erupted before and could become active again
The harrat are part of the Ring of Fire
questions.why: A volcano near Madinah erupted in 1256, so scientists watch for signs that magma is moving again.

wrong.A: The article says the 1256 lava stopped short of the city; nothing is flowing now.
wrong.B: The article does not mention selling rock.
wrong.D: The Ring of Fire is around the Pacific Ocean, not Arabia.

questions.stem: A volcano has thin, runny lava. What kind of eruption would scientists most likely expect?
options: A violent blast that hurls ash into the sky
A steady flow of lava moving downhill
No eruption of any kind, ever again
An eruption made only of gas
questions.why: The article says thin, runny lava lets gas escape easily, so it flows steadily downhill.

wrong.A: Violent blasts come from thick, sticky magma.
wrong.C: Runny lava still erupts; it just erupts calmly.
wrong.D: The article says runny lava pours out, so it is not only gas.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the paragraph about how volcanoes erupt?
options: Problem and solution
Time order
Question and answer
Compare and contrast
questions.why: The paragraph shows how explosive eruptions and calm eruptions are different and explains why.

wrong.A: The paragraph does not present a problem and a fix.
wrong.B: The paragraph is not a list of events in time order.
wrong.C: The paragraph does not ask and answer questions.

MID.prompt: Compare explosive eruptions and calm eruptions. What makes them different? Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I described both kinds of eruptions.
I explained how the magma causes the difference.
I used at least two details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Explosive eruptions and calm eruptions look very different, and the molten rock inside each volcano explains why. Explosive eruptions happen when the magma is thick and sticky, so gas gets trapped inside until the built-up pressure bursts out, hurling ash and broken rock high into the sky. Calm eruptions happen when the magma is thin and runny, which lets gas escape easily so the lava just flows steadily downhill like a river. Most of these volcanoes form along a tectonic plate boundary, which is why scientists closely monitor the magma and gases at active volcanoes to predict what kind of eruption might happen next.

keyWords.definition: the thin, hard outer layer of the Earth
keyWords.example: Deep wells are drilled through the crust to reach water and oil.

keyWords.definition: thick and sticky, so it flows slowly
keyWords.example: Cold honey is so viscous that it barely drips from the spoon.

keyWords.definition: a scientist who studies rocks, the ground, and how the Earth changes
keyWords.example: The geologist explained how the desert cliffs had formed in layers.

keyWords.definition: to move people away from a dangerous place to somewhere safe
keyWords.example: During the fire drill, teachers helped evacuate every classroom in two minutes.

keyWords.definition: quiet or inactive for a long time, but able to become active again
keyWords.example: The seeds lay dormant in the dry soil until the rain came.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Saudi Arabia's harrat are the most dangerous volcanic fields anywhere on Earth today.
Explosive eruptions happen far more often than calm ones.
Satellites have replaced every other tool for watching volcanoes.
Plates and magma shape how volcanoes erupt, so scientists watch them closely.
questions.why: The article connects plate movement and magma to the location and style of eruptions, then explains how scientists monitor volcanoes, including in Arabia.

wrong.A: The article never ranks the harrat as the most dangerous.
wrong.B: The article does not compare how often each kind happens.
wrong.C: Satellites are one tool among several, alongside seismometers and gas studies.

questions.stem: The article says the magma is viscous. Which meaning fits best?
options: Extremely hot
Thick and sticky
Full of holes
Fast-moving
questions.why: The article explains viscous as meaning thick and sticky, which is why it traps gas.

wrong.A: All magma is hot; viscous describes how it flows.
wrong.C: The word does not describe holes.
wrong.D: Viscous material moves slowly, not quickly.

questions.stem: What happened at Harrat Lunayyir in 2009?
options: Small earthquakes led to evacuations, but no eruption followed
A huge eruption buried several villages under fresh, glowing lava
Lava flowed toward Madinah for several weeks
Geologists found the first hot spot ever recorded in Arabia
questions.why: The article says thousands of small earthquakes shook the area as magma moved, villages were evacuated for a time, and no eruption followed.

wrong.B: The article says no eruption followed.
wrong.C: The lava flow toward Madinah happened in 1256, not 2009.
wrong.D: The article does not say a hot spot was discovered there.

questions.stem: According to geologists, what is connected to the formation of the harrat?
options: The Pacific Plate passing over a hot spot
One plate sliding beneath another under Iceland
The slow widening of the Red Sea
Gas escaping from fissures near Madinah
questions.why: The article says geologists link the harrat to the widening of the Red Sea, which is separating Arabia from Africa.

wrong.A: This explains the Hawaiian Islands, not the harrat.
wrong.B: Under Iceland, plates pull apart; and Iceland is not linked to the harrat.
wrong.D: Escaping gas is a warning sign, not the cause of the lava fields.

questions.stem: Why might officials evacuate a town even if an eruption never happens?
options: Evacuations stop magma from rising
Lava always reaches nearby towns
Every town near any volcano must be emptied once a year by law
Warning signs show real risk, so leaving early is safer
questions.why: Scientists cannot be sure an eruption will happen, so acting on warning signs, as at Lunayyir, protects people.

wrong.A: Moving people does not affect the magma.
wrong.B: In 1256 the lava stopped short of Madinah, so it does not always reach towns.
wrong.C: The article describes evacuations only when warning signs change.

questions.stem: Which tools does the article say can detect whether the ground is swelling?
options: Satellites and ground sensors
Seismometers placed directly inside the flowing lava
Thermometers dropped into craters
Cameras that photograph ash clouds
questions.why: The article names satellites and ground sensors as the tools that detect swelling.

wrong.B: Seismometers record earthquakes, and they are not placed in lava.
wrong.C: The article does not mention thermometers.
wrong.D: The article does not mention cameras.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the 1256 eruption near Madinah?
options: To prove that lava always stops before reaching a city
To explain how the Ring of Fire formed
To show that eruptions have affected Arabia in recorded history
To argue that every family should move out of the city of Madinah
questions.why: The 1256 eruption is a dated, real example showing that volcanoes in Arabia are not only from the distant past.

wrong.A: One example cannot prove that lava always stops.
wrong.B: The Ring of Fire is around the Pacific, not Arabia.
wrong.D: The author does not argue that anyone should leave the city.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the idea that dormant volcanoes still need to be watched?
options: Fresh lava glows red and orange
Magma can collect underground and make the ground swell
Tectonic plates move a few centimeters each year
The Ring of Fire surrounds the Pacific Ocean on nearly every side
questions.why: If magma can quietly collect below a volcano, a quiet volcano may be getting ready to erupt, so it still needs monitoring.

wrong.A: Lava color does not show that a quiet volcano could wake up.
wrong.C: Plate speed does not explain why dormant volcanoes need watching.
wrong.D: The location of the Ring of Fire is not evidence about dormant volcanoes.

HIGH.prompt: Should towns be built near the harrat of western Saudi Arabia? Take a position and support it with evidence about the region's history and how scientists monitor volcanoes.
checklist: I stated a clear position in my first sentence.
I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how each piece of evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think towns should be built near the harrat of western Saudi Arabia only with great caution, because the region's history and ongoing monitoring show both risk and relative safety. In 1256, a volcano near Madinah produced viscous lava that flowed toward the city but fortunately stopped short of it, proving that these volcanoes in the Earth's crust are not entirely dormant and can still threaten nearby communities. However, geologists in the Kingdom now closely monitor the harrat using instruments that detect small earthquakes and swelling ground, so if warning signs appear, officials would have time to evacuate residents before real danger arrives. Because of this careful monitoring, I believe towns can exist near the harrat as long as safety plans and evacuation routes stay ready at all times.
